overview: Medieval Brittany grew through changing kingdoms and a duchy on the Atlantic edge of Europe. Its towns, farms and multilingual communities supported an ambitious ducal court. The imported outline omits Nantes and parts of the historical duchy. Its 800 to 1600 span includes independent rule and the period after union with France.

periods.title: Kings and disruption
periods.summary: Ninth-century rulers enlarged Breton power. Viking attacks later disrupted its political institutions.

periods.title: The duchy
periods.summary: Ducal authority was restored and developed over centuries, alongside powerful lords and towns.

periods.title: A province of France
periods.summary: Union changed Brittany’s political status. The map continues to 1600, not a separate ducal fall date.

items.text: Jean IV’s castle of the Hermine at Vannes, begun around 1380, combined residence and fortification. Excavation recovered decorated floor tiles and substantial walls. Palace comfort depended on builders, carpenters and water engineers as much as impressive heraldry.

Castle latrines had passages separating them from living spaces. Waste conduits ran through the walls toward pits and the moat. A grand address did not remove the need to think about where the toilet went, or what happened afterwards.

Water diverted from the Marle powered a mill integrated into the castle. Wet deposits preserved wooden objects, while excavators also found tableware, rings, jew’s harps and a bone recorder fragment. The palace’s remains include work, meals and music.

sections.title: The pots that fed a town

items.text: Potters at Chartres-de-Bretagne supplied Rennes from the late tenth century, expanding production strongly in the eleventh to thirteenth centuries. Local raw materials produced pale, hard pottery well suited to cooking. Everyday technical choices helped fill thousands of kitchens.

A rounded cooking pot called an oule could prepare food over heat. Jugs carried and poured liquids, while bowls helped with food preparation and dairy products. The medieval pottery range was practical rather than a table setting with a special dish for every course.

Excavators found masses of pottery spoiled during firing at the workshops. These rejected pieces reveal what the potters made and how they worked. A failed pot could be bad news for its maker but excellent evidence for an archaeologist.

sections.title: When the town paid for visitors

items.text: Rennes’s fifteenth-century accounts record the practical cost of receiving ambassadors: lodging, transport, firewood, candles and even laundry. In 1475 some English visitors stayed with residents and others in inns. Diplomacy created plenty of work away from the negotiating table.

Official banquets might serve many kinds of meat, fish during fasting periods, sauces, pastries and seasonal fruit. These were expensive displays for important guests. They describe courtly hospitality rather than the daily dinner of a Breton farming family.

Bread could accompany the food or serve as an edible support in place of a plate. Musicians and entertainers appeared between courses. The accounts let us glimpse the occasion, though they do not preserve every seating plan or number of guests.

A dictionary printed at Tréguier on 5 November 1499 describes itself as “en troys langaiges”, meaning “in three languages”. This historical French wording comes from the Catholicon’s title. Its three languages were Breton, French and Latin, a useful combination in a multilingual society.

The Catholicon connects manuscript scholarship with early printing: Jehan Lagadec supplied the text and Jehan Calvez printed the 1499 edition. A dictionary made words easier to compare and study. It also reminds us that the language spoken at home need not match the language of a learned book.

sections.title: Cloth and connections across the sea

items.text: By the fifteenth century, fine linen from the area around Quintin, Uzel and Loudéac travelled to Spain. Castilian merchants settled in Nantes and built family connections through marriage and godparenthood. Maritime trade involved households and relationships as well as cargo.

ending.text: Union with France in 1532 turned the duchy into a province while preserving its territorial identity and particular institutions. Breton communities and languages continued. The imported endpoint 1600 is a map interval, not the disappearance of Brittany.
